findings.title: The name as a performed invocation
findings.claim: The focus's name clause can resonate as a performed invocation: wider verses call upon Allah or al-Rahman, remember the Lord's name, and place Allah's name formula at the start or threshold of particular acts.
findings.mechanism: In the focus, bi-ismi makes the divine name the means of beginning the utterance. The supplied wider texts make that name something called or remembered (17:110, 7:180, 73:8), mentioned over food (6:118), used in a statement from Solomon (27:30), and joined to a vessel's course and mooring (11:41). These distinct acts return through the focus's ism and Allah, giving the opening phrase a practical use in speech and action.
findings.reader_payoff: The opening remains a naming formula while becoming newly perceptible as an utterance that can accompany worship, communication, and ordinary action.
findings.containment: These are separate contexts, not a universal rule or one uniform ritual. The text at 6:118 mentions Allah's name over food without specifying this full prefatory formula; 11:41 uses only part of the focus formula, while 27:30 repeats the full formula in one message.

epistemic.reason: The exact target Arabic and connection notes supply explicit acts of calling, remembering, and naming, but connection targets have no word-level morphology; the divine-name branch used for direct invocation is itself qualified in the registry.

branch_activations.branch_gloss: ad, adlandırma ve ad ya da nitelik bakımından denklik
branch_activations.facet_statement: Ad, bir varlığı tanıtan ve ondan söz etmeyi sağlayan söz veya anlamdır.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus noun ism in bi-ismi Allah, the designation through which Allah is named.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 17:110 calls Allah or al-Rahman in prayer; 7:180 calls God through His names; 73:8 directs remembrance of the Lord's name; 6:118 mentions Allah's name over food; 27:30 repeats the full formula in a statement from Solomon; and 11:41 uses the name formula with the vessel's course and mooring.
branch_activations.activation: The separate acts of calling, remembering, and placing the name formula at a concrete action meet the focus noun ism. That contact moves the name from identification alone into an uttered invocation that accompanies speech and action.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The opening's name clause can be heard as a performed invocation that marks particular speech and acts with divine address.
branch_activations.boundary: The contexts do not make every use of the name the same act, and they do not establish a requirement to recite this exact formula before every action.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Dalın merkezinde, Yaratıcıyı başkalarından ayırarak gösteren ve yalnız ona özgü sayılan özel ad bulunur.
branch_activations.carrier: Allah as the focus's divine proper name.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 17:110 explicitly names Allah and al-Rahman as names by which God is called.
branch_activations.activation: The focus proper name Allah meets the independent call to address God by name, giving the named referent an invoked role in the focus formula.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The proper name in the opening can be heard as part of an address to the Creator, not only as an identifier.
branch_activations.boundary: The focus phrase does not itself state the later verse's prayer instructions or its treatment of recitation volume.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Özel adın doğrudan ya da seslenme öğesi yerine geçen bir sonla kullanılması, yakarma ve dilek bildiren seslenme biçimleri kurar.
branch_activations.carrier: Allah, named in the focus's bi-ismi Allah construction.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 17:110 says to call Allah or al-Rahman; 7:180 directs calling God through His names.
branch_activations.activation: The direct calls in the wider contexts meet the focus's proper-name carrier and activate the branch's address use, so the opening's naming can participate in invocation.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The phrase can be heard as an invocation through the divine name while retaining its ordinary naming construction.
branch_activations.boundary: The focus uses a prepositional name phrase, not a direct vocative; the address function is supplied by the wider contexts.

findings.title: A singular, honored name
findings.claim: The focus's divine name can carry a wider resonance of singular dignity: one verse asks whether the Lord has any namesake, while another calls the Lord's name blessed and pairs it with majesty and honor.
findings.mechanism: Allah is the proper-name carrier in the focus, and ism is the designation carrier. In 19:65 the Lord is presented as the one to be worshipped and the text asks whether He has any namesake; in 55:78 the Lord's name itself is called blessed and joined to majesty and honor. These independent predicates return through the focus's name relation and make the designation more than a neutral label.
findings.reader_payoff: The name in the opening becomes perceptible as both singularly referential and itself honored.
findings.containment: The focus itself does not state the no-namesake boundary or the later majesty language. These contexts add a limited resonance; they do not establish that uttering the name causes exaltation or determine the source derivation of ism.

epistemic.reason: Both supplied contexts explicitly relate the Lord or His name to uniqueness or honor, but target morphology is absent and the proper-name branch is qualified in the registry.

branch_activations.independent_trigger: 19:65 names the Lord of the heavens and earth, commands worship of Him, and asks whether He has any namesake.
branch_activations.activation: The focus proper name returns through the supplied no-namesake question, making the named referent's distinctness explicit in the wider context.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The opening's divine name can be heard as naming the one presented elsewhere as without a namesake.
branch_activations.boundary: The focus names Allah but does not itself state the no-namesake proposition.

branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus's naming formula can resonate as an honor-bearing mention of the Lord.
branch_activations.boundary: This is a relation supplied by one wider phrase; it does not say that the focus word itself means majesty or that saying the name changes God's status.

findings.title: Mercy as committed care
findings.claim: The focus's mercy names can resonate globally as active, self-bound care with wide reach: other verses say that God has written mercy upon Himself, that it encompasses all things, and that it is near to those who call and do good.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries the locally selected mercy sense in al-Rahman and al-Rahim. In 6:12 and 6:54 mercy is written upon God's own self; 7:156 joins its broad reach to a further act of writing it for a described group; 7:56 places God's mercy near those who call with fear and hope and act well. These independent scope and action cues meet the focus mercy terms and change them from a bare attribute into an enacted relation.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive the mercy names as naming care that acts, reaches outward, and is approached through conduct.
findings.containment: The wider passages do not assign separate functions to al-Rahman and al-Rahim or promise identical outcomes in every setting. The focus remains the opening naming formula; its wider resonance comes from these separate descriptions of mercy.

epistemic.reason: The supplied Arabic explicitly connects divine mercy with self-description, breadth, supplication, and good conduct, but the connection targets have no word-level morphology and the synthesis remains contextual.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Bu iç yöneliş, acınan kişiyi esirgemeyi ve ona iyilikte bulunmayı gerektiren etkin bir sonuç taşır.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus's two mercy epithets, locally used of God.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 6:12 and 6:54 say God wrote mercy upon Himself; 7:156 says His mercy encompasses everything and that He will write it for a described group; 7:56 joins God's mercy to calling in fear and hope and to good conduct.
branch_activations.activation: The focus mercy carriers meet the wider texts' explicit acts, reach, and conditions of mercy. The contact gives the adjectives an active beneficence reading while leaving their ordinary mercy sense intact.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The opening's mercy names can be heard as naming care that is declared, enacted, and broadly reaching.
branch_activations.boundary: The later acts and scope belong to their own contexts; they do not map one action to each epithet or settle how every instance of mercy operates.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Tanrı hakkında kullanıldığında esirgemenin genişliği ve yaratılmışlara iyilik olarak ulaşması belirginleşir.
branch_activations.carrier: The divine-use focus epithets al-Rahman and al-Rahim.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: The supplied contexts describe mercy as written upon God, reaching all things, near to those who call and do good, and written for a described group.
branch_activations.activation: These explicit wider descriptions of God's mercy meet the focus's divine mercy names; they activate the branch's God-use facet as an outward-reaching, beneficent relation.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus can carry a contextual sense of divine mercy as broad beneficence that also appears in particular responses.
branch_activations.boundary: The contextual descriptions do not supply a complete doctrine of mercy or define the distinct contribution of each focus epithet.

findings.title: Mercy as social conduct
findings.claim: The focus's mercy can resonate as care enacted among people: a wider passage joins close kinship to giving, forgiveness, and pardon and closes by naming Allah as Forgiving and Merciful; another identifies humble walking and peaceful reply as conduct of the servants of al-Rahman.
findings.mechanism: The focus epithets carry mercy. In 24:22, relatives are named among those to whom generosity is due, forgiveness and pardon are urged, and Allah is called Forgiving and Rahim; in 25:63, servants of al-Rahman are described through humble conduct and peaceful speech. Those acts return through the focus mercy terms and make mercy legible as a social practice, with kinship as one explicit setting.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the opening's mercy names resonate with how people forgive, give, and answer one another, not only with a divine attribute.
findings.containment: These later verses supply their own social instructions and descriptions; the focus itself does not command them. The kinship branch is a contextual root resonance, not a claim that God is literally a relative or that all social conduct is reducible to family ties.

epistemic.reason: 24:22 explicitly combines kinship, pardon, and Allah's name al-Rahim; 25:63 explicitly describes conduct associated with al-Rahman. The social synthesis is contextual, with no supplied target morphology.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Bu iç yöneliş, acınan kişiyi esirgemeyi ve ona iyilikte bulunmayı gerektiren etkin bir sonuç taşır.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus's two mercy epithets as the divine names al-Rahman and al-Rahim.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 24:22 urges giving to relatives and others, then forgiveness and pardon; 25:63 describes servants of al-Rahman as walking humbly and answering an ignorant address with peace.
branch_activations.activation: The independent practices of pardon, generosity, and peaceful response meet the focus mercy carriers. They let the mercy branch's active result appear as a way of treating others.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The opening mercy names can resonate with mercy enacted through giving, forgiving, and gentle speech.
branch_activations.boundary: The verses describe particular social practices; they do not make the focus itself an instruction to perform them or claim that these are the only forms of mercy.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Topluluğun bireylerinin birbirine acıyıp birbirini esirgemesi, çekirdeğin karşılıklı bir kuruluşta gerçekleşmesidir.

branch_activations.boundary: The source texts show particular examples; they do not establish a universal social program or replace the focus's divine-name construction.

branch_activations.boundary: The branch does not make Rahman or Rahim mean 'relative' in the focus and does not make the divine referent a member of a human lineage.

findings.title: A womb image within mercy
findings.claim: An exploratory global resonance lets the focus's mercy names carry an image of life held and formed in a womb.
findings.mechanism: The focus words al-Rahman and al-Rahim carry the locally selected mercy sense while sharing a root that includes the womb branch. The wider text at 22:5 traces created life through developmental stages, says forms are kept in wombs until a term, and then describes emergence and maturation. That separate containment-and-growth image returns through the focus root and can tint the mercy names with life-carrying care.
findings.reader_payoff: The mercy named at the opening becomes newly imaginable as care that surrounds and carries life toward emergence.
findings.containment: This does not claim that the focus adjectives lexically mean 'womb', that the divine referent has a body, or that this root image is primary. The 22:5 connection contains reciprocal counterevidence that root-only reproductive or landscape material does not clarify the focus, so this remains exploratory and relies on its explicit womb-and-development sequence.

epistemic.reason: The supplied 22:5 Arabic gives an independent womb and development image, but the connection carries only reciprocal counterevidence, target morphology is absent, and the root-level return is uncertain.

branch_activations.resulting_reading: Alongside mercy as beneficence, the opening can carry a root-level resonance of care that contains and carries life.
branch_activations.boundary: The connection itself records a no-value source assessment of root-only reproductive material; this activation depends on the supplied womb-and-growth image, remains exploratory, and is not a lexical gloss for the focus.

findings.title: Mercy as guidance and aid
findings.claim: The focus's al-Rahman can resonate as a source of guidance and aid: one wider verse names the Lord as al-Rahman before commands to follow and obey, while another pairs al-Rahman with an appeal for judgment and sought help.
findings.mechanism: The focus carrier al-Rahman meets the independent acts in 20:90 and 21:112. In the first, the Lord is named al-Rahman immediately before following and obedience are urged; in the second, the speaker asks the Lord to judge truthfully and calls the Rahman the one whose help is sought. The contact gives the focus name a relational role in both guidance and dependence.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the mercy name as a source approached for help and as a name under which following guidance becomes intelligible.
findings.containment: These are distinct later scenes, not commands or petitions stated by the focus itself. They do not turn the mercy name into a synonym for obedience or aid, and the two focus epithets are not assigned ranked or separate meanings.

epistemic.reason: The exact supplied texts explicitly place al-Rahman beside obedience and sought help, but the contextual relation is not encoded in the focus grammar and target morphology is unavailable.
